### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

#### **1.1 Introduction** 

According to our estimates, demand growth weakened sharply over the close of 2011, with the slowdown in conditions in Europe, not surprisingly, particularly pronounced.  Our analysis suggests that the weakness in demand has been carried over to the first quarter of this year, with fears over a faster than expected slowdown in Chinese demand adding to ongoing concerns over mature economy consumption. 

The weaker demand environment has, however, had little impact on prices, with the monthly average price registering five successive month-on-month gains from the October 2011 low of $7,348/tonne to $8,457/ tonne in March.  During the first quarter, copper traded a $7,471-8,658/tonne range and averaged $8,310/ tonne, up 11% on the final three months of last year. Many other aspects of the market balance were positive in this period.  Supply disruptions continued to be a feature against the background of what already was an exceptionally tight concentrate market, while reported inventories remained at low levels. 

figure, which confirmed the slowdown in the rate of growth.  Nevertheless prices at the end of April were comfortably above $8,000/tonne, again reinforcing the good underlying fundamentals of the red metal. 

In some respects the data specifically relating to the Chinese copper market has been positive with net imports of refined metal more than doubling year-onyear in the first quarter.  Also, copper semis production in the first quarter was running around 18% ahead of last year, although we believe that this initial figure may overestimate the increase.  The data relating to some of copper end use markets is, however, less encouraging.  The production of automobiles, air conditioning units, telecommunication and power cable all registered little growth, or year-on-year declines, up to March.  In addition, inventories of some of the downstream products, particularly within the air conditioning sector, have risen.  More importantly, there has been a build up of stocks of refined metal as imports have continued to flow into the country and as domestic production has risen sharply. 

Prices came under pressure in April, briefly dipping below $8,000/tonne on concerns about the potential for slower demand growth.  The market had to absorb the news of an official downgrade of the growth target by the Chinese government from 8% to 7.5%, and more recently a number of economic statistics – monthly industrial production and fixed asset investment numbers, and the first quarter GDP 

Thomson Reuters GFMS understands that a destocking exercise is already underway and this will have an immediate impact on the market by lower imports and higher exports of metal.  However, once this process of inventory adjustment is complete, we expect that China will provide a boost to the market in the second half of the year.

The demand and macroeconomic environment has filtered through to investment activity. Our understanding is that whilst the focus of the investment funds is more on broader economic themes rather copper’s individual fundamentals, the latter is nevertheless still relevant. We believe that this sector has been broadly neutral so far this year as optimism surrounding copper’s tight supply position has been dampened by ongoing demand (and broader macroeconomic) concerns. For the short term, we believe that such trends will remain in place, although continued monetary easing in Europe, North America and China (particularly in the face of weakening economic indicators), should limit the downside and support buying on dips, before a broader improvement in economic conditions over the second half adds upward momentum to prices. #### **1.2 Economic Assumptions** The outlook for copper consumption in the short-term has deteriorated since our previous _Three Year Copper Forecast_ . The nature and the source of concern has shifted somewhat in that the focus of the market late in the first quarter, and early in the second quarter, has been on the prospects for slower growth in China rather than on the debt position with the Eurozone. Our favoured indicator is the comprehensive, OECD composite leading indicator (CLI). As highlighted in the chart above, the OECD CLI is normally a good barometer for copper prices. This index has risen for four months in a row to 100.5 in February, up from the 2011 low of 100 in October. However, as discussed in Section 2, many of the other forward-looking indicators that we track are more bearish for copper. Real global GDP growth under our **base case scenario** is expected to fall to 2.3% this year due to a further deterioration in the Eurozone debt

crisis and its impact on developed and developing countries’ growth rates. Looking ahead, we expect to see a gradual improvement in the world economy over the following two years, with expansionary monetary policies remaining in place in key countries and the possible implementation of other global reflationary measures during this period. As a result, the world economy is forecast to grow at 3.0% and 3.5% in 2013 and 2014 respectively. **Scenario B** features a more positive tone for world GDP growth, which is projected to average 3.3% per annum over the forecast period. Central to this scenario are policies implemented by the US government and the Federal Reserve, in particular expansionary fiscal policies and ultra-loose monetary conditions. Nevertheless, higher economic growth should be achieved at the expense of rising US inflation, which is forecast to increase from 3.6% in 2012 to 5.8% by the end of the forecast period (annual averages in each case). Under such circumstances, we would expect to see the US dollar weakening from an annual average of $1.31/€ in 2012 to $1.40/€ by the end of the forecast. Under the more bearish **Scenario C** , we expect to see a sluggish economic performance, particularly in the developed world, as the governments struggle to get to grips with the still high levels of debt. The key factor to remember is that these problems are not restricted to just the smaller southern European economies, but include most of major copper consuming countries, with the obvious exception of China. Global GDP growth is therefore forecast to average 2.3% per annum between 2012 and 2014 under this scenario. #### **1.3 The Dollar** The US dollar started to recover against the euro in September last year on the back of growing concerns over the prolonged Eurozone debt crisis. Following the failure of EU leaders in December 2011 to offer a definitive solution to the debt crisis, the dollar rally continued in early 2012. Although the euro has recovered some lost ground against the dollar, the measures undertaken so far will not resolve the debt crisis per se, as the downside risks to the Eurozone remain high. riven by macro events, sometimes by specific views on the Chinese economy, as well as by the individual fundamentals. The first two factors have generally seen investment activity move into neutral mode so far this year. Although there have been some high profile examples of individual funds actively shorting the market, we do not see this as part of a growing trend. The latter factor of copper’s positive underlying fundamentals and its greater liquidity continues to attract interest. However, the flip side is that copper’s strong macro credentials and its particular price premium over industry marginal costs makes the market vulnerable to macro-based selling if economic sentiment takes a turn for the worse. We believe that the market may have to absorb some bad news on both fronts – the macro data, particularly the purchasing mangers’ indices could encourage liquidation in the sector, while what we expect will be bearish Chinese trade data for copper and copper products could also put the market under pressure. However, under our base case scenario, we expect an improvement in economic activity in the second half of the year, which should see funds return with a long side bias. #### **1.5 Consumption** The outlook for global copper demand remains clouded by uncertainty. Whilst the weakness in the Eurozone dominated the headlines over the close of 2011, more recently, the focus has shifted towards a faster than expected slowdown in underlying Chinese consumption over the opening months of 2012. The latter has led to a significant build up in inventory within the country, at both the refined and downstream product stage, which in our view will serve to weigh on prices over the near term. **5** Three Year Copper Forecast - April 2012 **CONFIDENTIAL** expects global copper consumption growth to slow to 2.7%, from 3.9% in 2011. Weakness is expected to be particularly acute over the first half, with offtake projected to grow by just 1.0% year-on-year. We expect a broad improvement in demand conditions in the second half of this year, with global consumption projected to rise by almost 5.0% on a year-on-year basis over this period. This is, firstly, based on an expected improvement in Chinese demand, as an easing of policy s

tarts to filter through to boost consumption in key end use industries. In addition, the low base of the second half of 2011 should ensure that mature economy demand growth returns to positive territory over the second half of the year, despite ongoing weakness in the Eurozone. The uptrend seen over the second half of the year is expected to be carried over to 2013, when we project that global demand growth will accelerate to 3.7%. In the final year of our forecast period, we expect growth will settle back to 3.4%, taking consumption in 2014 to 21.866 million tonnes, up 10.3% (or over 2 million tonnes) on the 2011 total. Although many of the factors that have limited production growth in the past will remain an issue, the extended period of high prices enjoyed by the copper industry is starting to be reflected in new projects being commissioned. This together with brownfield increases (which is generally the preferred method of expansion), should ensure an acceleration in mine production growth over the forecast period with expansion of 3.7% in 2012, followed by 5.5% and 6.1% in 2013 and 2014. The excellent margins enjoyed by copper producers will encourage them to maximise output and to bring on additional capacity. Thomson Reuters GFMS has just published its _Copper Survey 2012_ . In this report, we provided details on changes in the industry cost curve. As discussed in more detail in Section 4, there has been a further upward shift in the curve due to higher costs of consumables, labour and lower grades. Thomson Reuters GFMS estimates that average production costs increased by 16% last year to $2,815/tonne, while the 90th percentile of cash operating costs now resides at $4,410/tonne, obviously well in excess of the prices prevailing at the end of April. The implications for the market of the margin over production costs are discussed in Section 1.7. #### **1.6 Production** There are a number of issues facing the supply side of the copper market over the forecast period. Most important is the level of mine production; the growth of which has been restricted by a myriad of structural and technical related issues. Thomson Reuters GFMS estimates that global mine production increased by 0.1% in 2011, which merely extended a sustained period of low growth. The figure below highlights how a variety of problems offset the attempts by the industry to raise output. The greater availability of concentrate is the main factor behind our forecast of a 12.8% increase to refined output in 2014 over 2011 to 21.866 million tonnes. In percentage terms, we project that the fastest growth out to 2014 will occur in Africa with the 40% advance almost solely focused on the African Copperbelt. In volume terms, Asia will continue to dominate the increase. Predictably China is forecast to account for the bulk of the increase (approximately one million tonnes). #### **1.7 Market outlook** The demand environment has deteriorated since our previous report and this is the main reason for changes in our historical market balance and projections out to 2014. Consumption finished 2011 on a weak note. As a result, Thomson Reuters GFMS has downgraded its estimates of consumption growth to 3.4%, from an earlier estimate of 3.9%. Our figure for refined production is largely unchanged at 19.56 million tonnes. Last year’s deficit now stands at 256,000 tonnes compared to 372,000 tonnes. This was not reflected in movements in reported stocks, which were largely unchanged implying some draw down in unreported stocks. We note the reverse of this situation so far this year, with an unreported stock build, especially in China. This may overhang the market during the remainder of the first half; however the combination of a pickup in Chinese demand and lower imports should see a reverse of this stockbuild in the second half of the year. For 2012, we still have the market in a deficit, of 85,000 tonnes, down marginally from our previous projection of 101,000 tonnes. Our view of the supply side remains unchanged in that the industry struggles to raise production levels due to a mixture of structural issues such as lower grades, and mine closures and operational problems – technical, weather and strikerelated losses. This restricted production growth last year to 3.0%. On a quarterly basis, prices in the first quarter were slightly higher than we expected. However, we have scaled back our forecasts for this year on the assumption that the combination of relatively weak demand, plus a macro environment that will increase risk aversion on the part of the investment community, will keep the market under pressure in the short term. However, a common feature of the copper market is that dips in prices have generally been seen as buying opportunities by physical buyers and investment funds. In the first quarter, this restricted the down side to $7,471/tonne. We project a low of $7,400/tonne in the second quarter and an average of $8,200/tonne. Our analysis of the underlying fundamentals suggest that the trend of “buying on dips” should be extended until it becomes clear that the market is finally unable able to absorb the extra production in the pipeline. This is more likely to be a feature of the second half of next year rather than this year. Although we have slightly reduced our second price half forecast, we are still predicting a significant recovery from the levels prevailing at the end of April. Our view of the fundamentals for 2013 is also little changed. We still have the market in rough balance projecting a surplus of 20,000 tonnes, compared to our previous forecast of a 15,000 deficit. ##### **Latin America** 

Chile continues to dominate refined production even though the country led the regional decline last year. Output fell by 151,000 tonnes (almost 5%) to 3.09 million tonnes in 2011, with output from both sources, concentrate and SX-EW, down on 2010.  The slippage in SX-EW production was mainly due to lower production at Quebrada Blanca (-26%) and El Abra (-14%). 

After the production problems in recent years there is the potential for increased production from higher utilisation rates; however no major additions to smelting and refining capacity are scheduled to come on stream.  In fact there could be slightly lower output, via the SX-EW route, from projects such as El Abra, Mihilla and Quebrada Blanca.  There is potential for the first copper from Antofagasta’s 80,000 tpy Antucoya SX-EW project due onstream in 2014 due to the low level of pre-stripping required at the deposit; however we have not included it in our supply projections. There is also the potential for the 30,000 tpy Caserones project (Pan Pacific and Mitsui) to come onstream; however we note the sharp rise in development costs at the operation, which could possibly delay the timing to beyond our forecast period. 

Peruvian production fell 8% last year with the ongoing closure of Doe Run’s La Oroya smelter, the most significant contributor to the decline, which appears unlikely to come back on line before 2013 at the earliest.
